Namecheap has been around since 2001, it's based in Phoenix, Arizona, and its cheapest hosting plan costs less than a cup of coffee each month. So, here is our honest Namecheap hosting review for 2026, written after going through its shared, WordPress, VPS and dedicated plans. We checked every plan page on 9 November 2026. Shared hosting starts at $2.28/mo on a yearly plan, after a free 30-day trial, and dedicated servers start at $37.66/mo for the first year. But one thing upfront. We didn't buy a plan or run speed tests for this review, so any speed or uptime claim below is Namecheap's, and I'll say so. I've been using WordPress since 2014, and I run several eCommerce sites of my own on it. When I look at a cheap host, I skip straight to the renewal price. And honestly, that's where Namecheap surprised me. Let's have a look. All prices in this review are in US dollars, as shown on namecheap.com on 9 November 2026. Taxes are extra, and the intro discounts don't apply to renewals. You Can Try It Free for 30 Days Right now, Namecheap lets you try any shared plan free for 30 days. It's one trial per account, and Namecheap calls it a limited-time offer. That's a nice way to set up WordPress, poke around cPanel and see if you like it before you pay anything. Unlimited Sites From Stellar Plus Up Stellar lets you host 3 websites with 20 GB of storage. Step up to Stellar Plus, which is $2.98 a month for the first year, and you get unlimited websites, unmetered storage and unlimited mailboxes. You also get Imunify360, a security tool with a malware scanner and firewall, plus free SSL that's set up for you. Free migration from another cPanel host is included too. Four Data Center Locations When you sign up, you pick a data center in the US, the UK, the Netherlands or Singapore. If most of your visitors are in the US, pick the US. Namecheap says its UK, Netherlands and Singapore data centers run on 100% renewable power, if that matters to you. A Real Managed WordPress Option If you don't want to deal with cPanel at all, there's EasyWP. It's Namecheap's own managed WordPress hosting , where each site runs in its own container and Namecheap handles updates, caching and backups. The Starter plan is $3.24 a month on a yearly plan and renews at $5.74. Namecheap Hosting Review: The Bads Now, cheap hosting always comes with some trade-offs. Here's what you should know. SSD, Not NVMe, on Shared Plans Namecheap's shared plans run on regular SSD storage. That's fine for a small blog, but some of the hosts we've reviewed lately, like InMotion and DreamHost, use faster NVMe drives on their cheapest plans. Namecheap's VPS and EasyWP plans do use NVMe. The Free Trial and the Refund Don't Mix Here's a catch. The 30-day money-back guarantee only works if you sign up without the free trial. So, it's one or the other. text: Namecheap Review 2026: We Priced Every Product - Here's Where It Earns Its Name (and Where It Doesn't) Elliot, BearHost July 29, 2026 | 10 min read Namecheap is one of the few budget hosts whose name is also its pitch, which invites an obvious question: cheap compared to what, and at what cost? After pricing all seven of its product lines - domains, Stellar shared hosting, EasyWP, VPS, Private Email, reseller hosting, and the FastVPN service - the answer is more interesting than the usual "good for domains, meh for hosting" summary you'll find on review roundups. TL;DR Namecheap is a genuinely honest discounter. Its renewal jumps are the mildest of the big three budget providers, its domain privacy is free forever rather than a first-year teaser, and its VPS renewal prices are printed at checkout instead of buried in a terms page. The trade-offs are real too - thin entry-tier VPS specs, no phone support anywhere, and a free-trial billing model that quietly converts to paid if you forget it. Overall: 4.1 / 5. The scorecard Category Score One-line verdict Domain registration 4.8 / 5 The best reason to use Namecheap - fair prices, free lifetime privacy Shared hosting (Stellar) 4.2 / 5 Cheapest renewals in the market; resources are modest WordPress hosting (EasyWP) 3.9 / 5 Solid managed product, less aggressively priced than rivals VPS hosting 3.5 / 5 Transparent pricing, thin entry specs, panels cost extra Private Email 4.4 / 5 $14.88/yr business email is quietly one of the best deals here Reseller hosting 4.0 / 5 cPanel/WHM + WHMCS included - a real reseller stack FastVPN 3.6 / 5 Great first-year price, steep relative jump at renewal Support 3.7 / 5 24/7 live chat that's genuinely responsive - but no phone, ever Overall 4.1 / 5 An honest budget host that is best at domains and email Domains: still the reason most people arrive Namecheap built its reputation as the anti-GoDaddy registrar, and in 2026 that's still deserved. A .com runs $11.28 for the first year ($6.79 on the recurring new-customer promo) and renews at $18.48 - not the market's absolute lowest, but competitive. What separates it is what's bundled: WHOIS privacy protection free for the life of the domain, free DNSSEC, and a domain panel that doesn't ambush you with upsells at checkout. Several big-name competitors still treat privacy as a first-year freebie that becomes a paid line item in year two; Namecheap made it permanent years ago and never walked it back. If domains are all you need, this is a 4.8 - the missing 0.2 is only because registrars like Cloudflare sell at cost with no markup at all, for users who need nothing else. Stellar shared hosting: the renewal math is the story The Stellar line is Namecheap's shared hosting: Stellar (~$2.28/mo intro, ~$4.48 renewal, 3 sites, 20 GB SSD), Stellar Plus (~$2.98 → ~$7.48, unlimited sites, unmetered SSD), and Stellar Business (~$4.98 → ~$11.98, 50 GB cloud storage plus Imunify360 security). Every tier carries a 30-day free trial, unmetered bandwidth, free migration, free SSL, the free Supersonic CDN, and a 100% uptime guarantee backed by account credits. That renewal column is where Namecheap quietly beats everyone. Hostinger's entry plan renews around $10.99, GoDaddy's at $11.99 - Stellar renews at $4.48. Over five years, that difference compounds into the cheapest ownership cost among the big three, which we ran the full numbers on in the Namecheap pricing breakdown . What keeps the score at 4.2 rather than higher: the resources are honest but modest (the entry tier's 20 GB and shared CPU suits blogs and brochure sites, not stores under load), and the 30-day-trial billing means the first charge arrives after you've stopped paying attention. Set a reminder. EasyWP: good product, middling deal EasyWP is Namecheap's managed WordPress platform, and it's a separate thing from running WordPress on a Stellar plan. Starter is free for the first month then $9.88/mo (10 GB NVMe, 50K visits), Turbo runs $13.88 → $18.88 (50 GB, 200K visits), and Supersonic $20.88 → $26.88 (100 GB, 500K visits, 99.99% uptime). All tiers include a free CDN, SSL, automatic updates, and unlimited bandwidth. The platform itself is pleasant - provisioning is fast, the dashboard is uncluttered, and the visit caps are generous for the price. The catch is context: Hostinger bundles managed WordPress into shared plans from $2.99, so EasyWP's value case rests on the managed experience rather than the sticker. (BearHost's WordPress hosting holds its price at renewal, for a third data point.) If you want WordPress cheap, Stellar runs it too; if you want it managed and tidy, EasyWP is fine at 3.9. VPS: transparent, but thin where it counts Namecheap's five VPS tiers run from Spark ($3.88/mo intro on yearly billing, renewing at $58.56/yr) to Hypernova ($46.88/mo, renewing at $634.56/yr), all on SSD RAID 10 with full root access. Two things deserve genuine credit: the renewal price is printed next to the intro price at checkout - rare honesty in this market - and yearly terms mean you're never locked in for the 3-4 years some competitors require. Now the critique, bias disclosed. Spark's 1 vCPU and 1 GB RAM is genuinely too little for most production workloads in 2026 - that's a monitoring node, not a web server. Control panels cost extra (Webuzo from $2.88/mo, cPanel from $17.88/mo, which can exceed the server itself), and management is user-responsible by default. Our own entry VPS is $4.49/mo with a dedicated KVM core and no renewal movement at all. Within Namecheap's own lineup, Pulsar ($6.88/mo, 2 vCPU/2 GB) is the honest starting point. Private Email: the sleeper deal Namecheap's Private Email is the product this review keeps wanting to talk about. Launch costs $14.88/yr for a mailbox after a 30-day trial - against roughly $72/yr for Microsoft 365's entry mailbox or $84/yr for Google Workspace. Expand ($41.88/yr, 3 mailboxes) and Scale ($71.88/yr, 5 mailboxes) keep the per-seat cost low, and the feature set - webmail, calendar, CalDAV/CardDAV, IMAP/SMTP/POP3, Jellyfish anti-spam, storage encryption - covers what a small business actually uses. It isn't Microsoft 365; there are no Office apps and the storage caps (5-15 GB per mailbox) are tight for email hoarders. But as domain-matched business email for a small operation, $14.88 a year is hard to argue with. 4.4. Reseller hosting: a real stack, not a checkbox The reseller line (Nebula, Galaxy Expert, Universe Pro) spans 25 to 150 cPanel accounts on 30-150 GB SSD, renewing between $19.88 and $58.88/mo. What makes it credible is the tooling: cPanel/WHM included free, a WHMCS billing license bundled (tiered up to 1,000 clients on the top plan), anonymous nameservers, white-label branding, and a choice of US or UK datacenter. That's the full stack an actual hosting reseller needs, at prices that leave margin to resell against. The audience is narrow - web agencies and hosting entrepreneurs - but for that audience it's one of the more complete budget reseller offers around. 4.0. FastVPN: fine product, watch the renewal FastVPN is the odd product out - a consumer VPN from a domain registrar. The numbers: $9.88 for the first year (then $34.56/yr), $7.88/mo month-to-month with a 30-day free trial, 2,700+ servers in 100+ locations, unlimited devices on privacy servers, and a no-logs policy. At the intro price it undercuts NordVPN, ExpressVPN, and Surfshark by a wide margin. The renewal is where the shine dulls: $9.88 to $34.56 is a 3.5x jump - ironically the exact pattern Namecheap avoids on its hosting products. It's still cheaper at renewal than most big-name VPNs, but the first-year price is doing heavy lifting in the marketing. If a VPN is a nice-to-have for you, it's a solid add-on; dedicated VPN providers still win on speed testing depth and audited no-log claims. 3.6. Support and reliability: the honest paragraph Namecheap's support is 24/7 live chat and tickets - and the chat is legitimately good: real humans, reasonable wait times, agents who can actually fix hosting issues rather than read scripts. What it has never offered is a phone number. If talking to a human voice during an outage matters to you, that's structural, not a bad day. On uptime: the Stellar line advertises a 100% uptime guarantee, which in practice is an SLA with service credits rather than a physics claim. EasyWP's stated targets (99.9% on Starter/Turbo, 99.99% on Supersonic) are the more meaningful numbers. Our experience watching this market: Namecheap's reliability is fine for its price class, without being the benchmark - the premium performance hosts still hold that ground. Who Namecheap is actually for? The pattern across all seven products: Namecheap is at its best when the product is simple and the pricing transparency does the work - domains, email, entry shared hosting, reseller accounts. It's at its weakest where raw resources decide the outcome - VPS entry tiers and performance-critical WordPress. So: buy the domains without hesitation. Take the Private Email deal if you need business email under ~5 seats. Use Stellar for small sites and enjoy the market's gentlest renewals. Think twice at the VPS tier if your workload is production-grade - compare specs before the checkout, whether that's against our plans or anyone else's. If you're already on Namecheap hosting and outgrowing it, the wider field is mapped in best Namecheap alternatives , with the GoDaddy head-to-head in Namecheap vs GoDaddy and the Hostinger one in Hostinger vs Namecheap . Conclusion Namecheap earns a 4.1: the rare budget provider whose cheapness is a pricing philosophy rather than a bait pattern. Domains and Private Email are close to best-in-market. Shared hosting wins on the renewal math that most reviews never run. The honest weaknesses - entry VPS specs, panels sold separately, chat-only support, auto-converting trials - are all visible before you buy, which is more than can be said for most of this industry. If those trade-offs fit your project, use it with confidence; if your workload needs more server than Namecheap's entry tiers offer, that's the one place we'd point you at a different kind of VPS - or at least at Pulsar rather than Spark.
